 # Connect 4: Power-Up Edition

An advanced connect four strategy game developed in C programming language that is more complex than the conventional version of connect four in terms of features and customization options.

---

## Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Key Components](#key-components)
- [Technical Architecture](#technical-architecture)
- [Getting Started](#getting-started)
  - [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
  - [Compilation](#compilation)
  - [Download Pre-compiled Binaries](#download-pre-compiled-binaries)

---

## Overview

The regular Connect 4 game has certain restrictions, such as being confined to 6x7 squares, using two players only from one place, and having no record keeping features. The game **Connect 4: Power-Up Edition** overcomes these problems by providing a menu-based modular C program that allows variable board size and incorporates power-ups for players.

---

## Key Components

### Game Modes
- **Player vs. Player (PvP):** Two-player local mode with customizable names and unique disc icons.
- **Player vs. Computer (PvC):** Single-player mode with two AI difficulty levels:
  - **Easy:** Randomly selects valid columns.
  - **Medium:** Analyzes the board in order to make immediate moves leading to a win or preventing opponent from winning.

### Customization & Rules
- **Dynamic Grid Settings:** Configure grid sizes (such as 8x9, 10x10) and select number of discs for winning sequence (4 or 5 discs).
- **Power-Ups:** Unique discs to use once per game:
  - **Bomb Disc:** Removes surrounding discs when placed.
  - **Anvil Disc:** Removes an entire column when placed.
- **Undo Feature:** Undo last move during gameplay session.

### Saving & Progression
- **Scoring & Best Streaks:** Points scored depend on board size, effectiveness of moves and difficulty of AI. Saves both best and all time win streaks.
- **Saving & Loading Games:** Ability to serialize current game and continue playing later sessions.
- **Leaderboard & History:** Save statistics on persistent storage including total wins, losses, scores, and best streaks.

---

## Technical Architecture

The program employs the standard C libraries such as stdio.h, string.h, time.h, and stdlib.h and exhibits several concepts of system programming:

| Concept | Implementation |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Dynamic Memory Allocation** | Dynamically creates two-dimensional array boards based on user-defined numbers of rows and columns. |
| **Recursion** | Line counting function scans rows, columns, and diagonals dynamically regardless of board size and win length. |
| **Structure and Pointers** | Bundles player information, match status, and moves performed. |
| **File Handling** | Performs data handling for saved matches, match logs, and game ranking. |
| **Input Validations** | Validates menu input and column input to avoid out-of-bound actions. |

---

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- **Operating System:** Windows, Linux, or macOS
- **Compiler:** GCC (MinGW on Windows, GCC on Linux, or Clang / Xcode Command Line Tools on macOS)
- **IDE (Optional):** Visual Studio Code or Dev-C++

### Compilation

First, clone the repository and navigate into the project folder:

```bash
git clone [https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4](https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4)
cd Connect4
```

Then compile and run based on your operating system:

| Operating System | Compile Command | Run Command |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Windows** | `gcc main.c -o connect4.exe` | `connect4.exe` |
| **Linux** | `gcc main.c -o connect4` | `./connect4` |
| **macOS** | `clang main.c -o connect4` (or `gcc main.c -o connect4`) | `./connect4` |

### Download Pre-compiled Binaries

In case you do not want to compile the source code yourself, pre-compiled binaries are available for Windows, Linux, and macOS in the [Releases](https://github.com/Asher-1971/Connect4/releases) section.

| Operating System | File | Instructions |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Windows** | `connect4-windows-x64.exe` | Just download and double-click to execute, or execute from Command Prompt. |
| **Linux** | `connect4-linux-x64` | Run `chmod +x connect4-linux-x64 && ./connect4-linux-x64`. |
| **macOS** | `connect4-macos-universal` | Run `chmod +x connect4-macos-universal && ./connect4-macos-universal`. |

  - **Anvil Disc:** Removes an entire column when placed.
- **Undo Feature:** Undo last move during gameplay session.

- **Scoring & Best Streaks:** Points scored depend on board size, effectiveness of moves and difficulty of AI. Saves both best and all time win streaks.

The program employs the standard C libraries such as stdio.h, string.h, time.h, and stdlib.h and exhibits several concepts of system programming:

| Concept | Implementation |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Dynamic Memory Allocation** | Dynamically creates two-dimensional array boards based on user-defined numbers of rows and columns. |
| **Recursion** | Line counting function scans rows, columns, and diagonals dynamically regardless of board size and win length. |
| **Structure and Pointers** | Bundles player information, match status, and moves performed. |
| **File Handling** | Performs data handling for saved matches, match logs, and game ranking. |

Your AI currently searches the same board positions repeatedly through different move orders. A transposition table caches:

- Alpha-beta bound
- Best move

- Negamax
- Alpha-beta pruning
- Iterative deepening
- Center-first move ordering
- Time budgets

- Normal AI searches deeper within 100 ms.
- Hard AI searches significantly deeper within 1000 ms.
- Fewer repeated calculations.
- Stronger tactical decisions.
- Faster response on larger boards.

2. Better move ordering using the cached best move
3. Immediate win/block checks before full search
4. Difficulty-specific evaluation/search settings
5. Longer-term: opening-book moves for standard 6×7 Connect Four

response.value:
A transposition table can support power-ups cleanly, but the **entire game state must be part of the cache key**.

Your current [`AIGameState`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h) already contains the important power-up fields:

```c
bool bomb_used[3];
bool anvil_used[3];
```

The hash must include:

- Every board cell
- Board dimensions
- Win length
- Current player
- Bomb-used status for Player 1 and Player 2
- Anvil-used status for Player 1 and Player 2
- Any future rule/configuration flags

A good design is a Zobrist hash:

```c
uint64_t hash_state(const AIGameState *state);
```

Each board piece and power-up flag receives a random key. The state hash is the XOR of all relevant keys.

### Transposition entry

```c
typedef struct {
    uint64_t hash;
    int depth;
    int score;
    int alpha;
    int beta;
    Move best_move;
    BoundType bound;
} TTEntry;
```

The cached `best_move` must include its type:

```c
typedef struct {
    int col;
    MoveType type;  // NORMAL, BOMB, or ANVIL
} Move;
```

That matters because:

```text
column 3 + normal move
```

is different from:

```text
column 3 + bomb move
```

### Example

These two states must produce different hashes:

```text
Same board
Same player
Same dimensions
```

but:

```text
State A: Player 1 has not used the bomb
State B: Player 1 already used the bomb
```

Otherwise, the AI could incorrectly reuse a result where a bomb move was legal when it is no longer legal.

### Power-up-specific concerns

#### Bombs

Bombs change several cells and then apply gravity. The resulting board must be hashed normally after the move. The cache does not need special bomb logic beyond including the updated board and `bomb_used` flags.

#### Anvils

Anvils remove a full column. Again, hash the resulting board and the updated `anvil_used` flag.

#### Move generation

The transposition table should store the full best move:

```c
best_move.col
best_move.type
```

Do not cache only the column.

#### Frontend bridge

When power-ups are enabled, [`getBestMove()`](/workspaces/Connect4/module3.h:78) must copy the frontend’s bomb/anvil usage state into `AIGameState`. Currently the bridge only copies the board, player, and move count.

### Important rule

The hash must also distinguish different rule configurations:

```text
Connect-4 vs Connect-5
6x7 board vs 10x10 board
Power-ups disabled vs enabled
```

Otherwise, cached results from one game configuration could contaminate another.

### Recommended architecture

```text
AIGameState
    ↓
Zobrist hash
    ↓
Transposition table lookup
    ↓
Negamax search
    ↓
Cache score, bound, and Move
```

So the transposition table is compatible with future power-ups. The key requirement is that it must cache the **complete state**, not just the board layout.

response.value:
```text
AI ARCHITECTURE AND TRANSPOSITION TABLE PLAN
================================================

1. Current Architecture

The project currently uses:

- Frontend state: GameState in header.h
- AI state: AIGameState in module3.h
- Move representation: Move containing col and MoveType
- Bridge: getBestMove() converts the frontend board into an AI board
- Search: negamax with alpha-beta pruning
- Move ordering: center-out column ordering
- Evaluation: weighted board windows and center proximity
- Time control: deadline_ms using monotonic time
- Power-up definitions: bomb_used and anvil_used fields already exist
- Power-up behavior: currently disabled by ENABLE_POWERUPS == 0
- Board limit: MAX_DIM == 20
- Win lengths: 4 or 5 in the current frontend
- AI difficulty:
  Easy: random legal move
  Normal: 100 ms search
  Hard: 1000 ms search

The architecture is modular enough for a transposition table because the
AI engine already operates on a complete AIGameState copy rather than
references to the frontend.

However, the frontend and AI are still separate representations:

Frontend:
- Character board
- '.' empty
- 'X' player 1
- 'O' player 2
- Top-down rows
- Separate boardColsFilled array
- move_count

AI:
- uint8_t board
- Bottom-up rows
- Numeric pieces
- current_player
- move_count
- power-up flags

The bridge is responsible for converting between these representations.
A transposition table should operate exclusively inside module3.c and
module3.h, not in start.c or game.c.

2. Main Architectural Limitation

A transposition table can only be correct if the cache key represents
the complete state.

The board alone is insufficient.

The key must include:

- Every board cell
- rows
- cols
- win_length
- current_player
- move_count
- bomb_used[1]
- bomb_used[2]
- anvil_used[1]
- anvil_used[2]
- ENABLE_POWERUPS
- Move and rule configuration

Move count should not be used as a primary key. It can be derived from
the board for normal moves, but power-ups can change the board without
changing the move count consistently unless it is explicitly stored.
Therefore, move_count should remain part of the cache identity.

A transposition entry must not be shared between configurations such as:

- 6x7, win length 4
- 6x7, win length 5
- 10x10, win length 5
- Power-ups disabled
- Power-ups enabled
- Any future special-rule configuration

The simplest safe design is to clear the table whenever a new game starts
or whenever the board dimensions, win length, or power-up configuration
change.

A Zobrist key can be used for each configuration, but random Zobrist keys
must be initialized once and used consistently for the whole application.
Do not regenerate keys inside each search.

3. Zobrist Hash Design

Create a Zobrist structure containing:

- Piece keys:
  zobrist_piece[MAX_DIM][MAX_DIM][3]

- Player key:
  zobrist_player[3]

- Dimension/configuration keys:
  zobrist_rows[MAX_DIM + 1]
  zobrist_cols[MAX_DIM + 1]
  zobrist_win_length[MAX_DIM + 1]
  zobrist_powerups_enabled
  zobrist_move_count[MAX_DIM * MAX_DIM + 1]

- Power-up keys:
  zobrist_bomb_used[3]
  zobrist_anvil_used[3]

For each state:

hash = 0
for every board cell:
    if board[r][c] != 0:
        hash ^= piece_keys[r][c][board[r][c]]

hash ^= player_keys[state->current_player]
hash ^= rows_key[state->rows]
hash ^= cols_key[state->cols]
hash ^= win_length_key[state->win_length]
hash ^= move_count_key[state->move_count]

if power-ups are enabled:
    hash ^= bomb_used_keys[player]
    hash ^= anvil_used_keys[player]

This can be made incremental:

- When a normal move is applied, XOR in the new piece.
- When a bomb/anvil changes cells, XOR removed pieces and new pieces.
- XOR the old player key and new player key.
- XOR the old/new move count key.
- XOR power-up usage keys when usage changes.

Incremental hashing is optional for the first implementation. Computing
the hash once per node is simple but slower. A parent-to-child hash
passed through negamax would be more efficient.

4. Transposition Entry

typedef enum {
    TT_EXACT,
    TT_LOWER_BOUND,
    TT_UPPER_BOUND
} TTBound;

typedef struct {
    uint64_t key;
    uint32_t generation;
    uint8_t depth;
    TTBound bound;
    int score;
    Move best_move;
} TTEntry;

Recommended fields:

- key:
  Zobrist hash or 64-bit primary key

- full_signature:
  Optional full state fingerprint or 128-bit hash

- depth:
  Depth from the node to terminal or leaf

- bound:
  Exact, lower, or upper

- score:
  Negamax evaluation for this state

- best_move:
  Column and MoveType

- generation:
  Search or game generation number

A 64-bit Zobrist hash can theoretically collide. For correctness, add
either:

- A full collision signature
- A 128-bit key
- Or a comparison against a canonical copy of the state

For this project, the simplest defensible implementation is:

- Zobrist 64-bit key as the table index
- Store the board signature or key separately
- Before using an entry, verify board_signature matches

A separate board signature also makes debugging easier.

If no collision verification is implemented, the table must be described
as a performance optimization only. It should never silently produce
incorrect moves due to hash collisions.

5. Integration with Existing Negamax

At the start of negamax:

1. Check valid_state(s).
2. Check ctx.
3. Check timeout.
4. Check terminal state.
5. Check TT.

The TT lookup should occur after terminal-state detection but before
move generation and evaluation.

Pseudo-code:

int negamax(AIGameState *state, int depth,
            int alpha, int beta, SearchContext *ctx)
{
    if (!valid_state(state) || !ctx)
        return 0;

    if (terminal state)
        return terminal score;

    TTEntry *entry = tt_lookup(state);

    if (entry != NULL && entry->depth >= depth)
    {
        if (entry->bound == TT_EXACT)
            return entry->score;

        if (entry->bound == TT_LOWER_BOUND && entry->score >= beta)
            return entry->score;

        if (entry->bound == TT_UPPER_BOUND && entry->score <= alpha)
            return entry->score;
    }

    if (depth <= 0)
        return evaluate_board(state);

    generate_moves(...);
    search in TT best move order;
    record alpha/beta result;
    return best_value;
}

Important: TT entries are depth-dependent.

Do not reuse:

- A 1-ply result as a 8-ply result
- An entry searched with an old win length
- An entry searched with a different power-up state
- An incomplete result obtained after timeout
- Entries from a previous game configuration

An entry only becomes reusable if:

- entry->depth >= requested_depth
- board/configuration key matches
- entry was completed

Timeouted searches must not be stored.

6. Alpha-Beta Bound Types

When storing a result:

- Exact:
  The node was searched with an alpha-beta window that did not produce
  a cutoff and the result is fully determined.

- Lower bound:
  A beta cutoff occurred, and the value is at least the stored score.

- Upper bound:
  No move raised alpha enough, or the search's window produced an
  upper-bound result.

Example:

original_alpha = alpha
original_beta = beta

search children

if best_value <= original_alpha:
    store TT_UPPER_BOUND
else if best_value >= original_beta:
    store TT_LOWER_BOUND
else:
    store TT_EXACT

This prevents the table from treating bounds as exact scores.

7. Move Ordering

The TT should store the best move from a completed depth.

When generating moves:

1. Look up TT best_move.
2. Search TT best_move first.
3. Search remaining moves center-outward.
4. If power-ups are enabled, avoid artificial ordering biases.

Promote principal variation:

- TT best move
- Immediate winning move
- Blocking move
- Center-outward moves
- Remaining moves

Power-ups should be ordered by game value, but do not remove normal
moves from the ordering.

Example TT move:

Move tt_move = { col: 3, type: MOVE_NORMAL };

If tt_move.type == MOVE_NORMAL:
    search that move first.

If the move is now illegal:
    ignore it and fall back to center-outward ordering.

This prevents stale TT moves from corrupting move generation.

8. Power-Up Compatibility

Power-ups are fully compatible if every state-changing field is in the
state key.

Board change:

- Bomb placement changes several board cells.
- Anvil placement removes an entire column.
- Gravity changes piece positions.
- Move count increases or remains unchanged depending on the power-up
  rules.
- Current player changes.
- Usage flags change.

All of these changes must be reflected in the next state's hash.

Normal move:

- Add one player piece.
- Increment move_count.
- Switch current_player.

Bomb move:

- Place or remove the affected board region according to the rule.
- Apply gravity if that is retained in your power-up specification.
- Set bomb_used[player] = true.
- Increment move_count.
- Switch current_player.

Anvil move:

- Clear the selected column.
- Set anvil_used[player] = true.
- Increment move_count.
- Switch current_player.

TT key requirements:

- board
- bomb_used
- anvil_used
- current_player
- move_count
- win_length
- rows
- cols
- power-up enabled flag
- move_count

The key must never depend on MoveType alone. MoveType is an action,
not a complete post-move state.

9. Frontend Bridge Changes

The bridge currently copies:

- board
- rows
- cols
- win_length
- current_player
- move_count

It does not copy frontend power-up flags.

When power-ups are enabled, extend the bridge API:

AIGameState ai = {0};

ai.bomb_used[1] = fe->bomb_used[1];
ai.bomb_used[2] = fe->bomb_used[2];

ai.anvil_used[1] = fe->anvil_used[1];
ai.anvil_used[2] = fe->anvil_used[2];

ai.powerups_enabled = ENABLE_POWERUPS;

This is not safe yet because GameState does not contain power-up usage
fields. They must be added to the frontend state and initialized for
each new game, then copied during every getBestMove() call.

The frontend save/load format must also persist:

- bomb_used
- anvil_used
- move count
- turn
- board
- board dimensions
- win length
- game mode
- AI difficulty

10. Limitations with the Existing Architecture

10.1 Fixed board arrays

AIGameState is fixed to MAX_DIM * MAX_DIM.

This is simple and stack friendly, but it:

- Limits future dimensions
- Repeats large state copies
- Makes transposition memory larger
- Prevents easy custom board implementations above 20

It is adequate for the current 4-20 range.

10.2 Stack-allocated copy-make

try_apply_move() copies the complete AIGameState:

- 20x20 board
- ~400 bytes
- Additional metadata
- Power-up fields

400 bytes per move is small for 20x20 in C, but the negamax tree copies
states repeatedly.

The transposition table reduces repeated search, but copy-make remains
more expensive than in-place move/unmove.

10.3 No direct TT inside the frontend

The TT belongs in module3.c.

game.c should not know TT entries.

start.c should not know TT entries.

getBestMove() should remain the only frontend-to-AI bridge.

10.4 Search time is wall-clock based

The TT can store a position from an old search depth.

Iterative deepening will reuse TT entries when they represent completed
search depths.

However, TT entries must never be used across games that have the same
Zobrist key but different search rules.

A TT generation number should isolate games.

10.5 Evaluator state assumptions

evaluate_board() assumes valid state.

valid_state() should remain the authority for:

- dimensions
- win length
- current player
- move count
- gravity
- piece counts
- power-up flags

TT lookup must occur only after valid_state() succeeds.

10.6 Terminal states

Terminal states must not generate moves.

The TT lookup should not store child scores for an already terminal root.

find_best_move() already rejects terminal roots.

A terminal TT entry can be stored as an exact mate score, but mate scores
should include depth if used across iterative deepening.

11. Difficulty Integration

Easy:

- Keep random move selection.
- Do not create TT entries.
- No search needed.

Normal:

- 100 ms search.
- TT enabled.
- Use TT best move.
- Maximum depth can be controlled by remaining cells.

Hard:

- 1000 ms search.
- TT enabled.
- Use TT best move.
- Search extra completed depths.
- Prefer exact and completed entries.

Recommended implementation:

#define AI_NORMAL_TIME_MS 100
#define AI_HARD_TIME_MS 1000

The TT should not change move behavior between identical positions
and identical budgets. It should make the search faster, not alter
the mathematical evaluation.

12. Memory and Table Size

Recommended initial limits:

- TT entries: 262144
- Approximate memory:
  Entry size approximately 32-64 bytes
- 8-16 MB depending on padding

For a student project:

#define TT_SIZE 65536

would be sufficient for 6x7 and 4x4 tests.

For 20x20:

#define TT_SIZE 262144
or higher if hardware allows.

Because hash tables are fixed-size, replacement is important:

- Replace by depth:
  Keep deeper entries.
- Replace older entries:
  Keep entries from the latest generation.
- Replace exact entries over bounds:
  Preserve exact information.
- Never evict entries mid-search permanently if they are useful.
- Keep direct-mapped or 4-way set associative entries.

13. Replacement Policy

The recommended policy:

1. If the table slot is empty:
   store entry.

2. If the stored key is equal:
   replace if:
   - new entry depth is greater
   - or new entry is exact
   - or generation is newer

3. If the key differs:
   replace only if:
   - new depth is greater than old depth
   - or old entry generation is older
   - or old entry is terminal/incomplete
   - otherwise keep old entry

This is more useful than random replacement.

14. Table Lifecycle

Before a game:

- tt_clear()
- reset generation
- initialize Zobrist keys

Before each AI move:

- Increment search generation
- Optionally clear entries when the state/configuration changes
- Set SearchContext deadline

After search:

- Preserve completed TT entries
- Discard timed-out entries
- Keep only entries with a valid bound
- Clear when a new game is initialized

The TT should not survive save/load unless the loaded state plus
configuration are also restored and Zobrist keys remain identical.

For simplicity:

- Clear on every load
- Clear on every new game
- Clear on board-size or win-length change
- Clear on AI difficulty change only if generation rules change

15. Testing Plan

Phase 1: Hash correctness

Test:

- Equal states produce equal keys
- Same board with different player produces different keys
- Same board with different win length produces different keys
- Same board with different dimensions produces different keys
- Bomb used state is different
- Anvil used state is different
- Normal move updates hash correctly
- Bomb move updates hash correctly
- Anvil move updates hash correctly
- Incremental hash equals recomputed hash

Phase 2: TT correctness

Test:

- TT exact hit
- TT lower-bound hit
- TT upper-bound hit
- TT depth replacement
- TT stale move replacement
- TT timeout doesn't store incomplete score
- TT terminal state no move
- TT disabled vs enabled rules
- 4x4 positions
- 6x7 positions
- 20x20 positions
- Random legal states
- Random power-up states

Phase 3: Negamax oracle

Compare TT-enabled negamax against TT-disabled negamax:

- Same position
- Same depth
- Same alpha/beta
- Same move ordering
- Same random seed for Easy

The TT-enabled result must exactly match the TT-disabled result
for completed searches.

Phase 4: Board-independent oracle

Compare check_winner() against an independent brute-force line scan
on every 4x4 and 6x7 sample state.

Phase 5: Power-ups

Test:

- Bomb-used flag changes key
- Bomb move produces same result as recomputing state
- Anvil-used flag changes key
- Gravity after bomb is reflected in hash
- TT best move is MoveType-aware
- TT never reuses a bomb move after bomb_used becomes true
- TT never reuses an anvil move after anvil_used becomes true

16. Known Incomplete Areas

The current framework cannot fully support power-ups until:

- GameState contains bomb/anvil usage
- getBestMove() copies those flags
- try_apply_move() has complete bomb/anvil behavior
- generate_moves() creates bomb/anvil Move entries
- Save/load persists power-up state
- UI exposes power-up selection
- TT stores MoveType

The TT itself does not need to change to support power-ups if the
AIGameState is designed as the single source of truth.

17. Strength and Limits

A TT can improve strength because it:

- Reduces repeated node calculations
- Enables deeper search at fixed time
- Preserves best moves from iterative deepening
- Improves move ordering
- Helps with repeated tactical positions
- Makes 100 ms Normal and 1000 ms Hard more efficient

It does not:

- Make the evaluator more tactically intelligent
- Add a strategic opening book
- Correct invalid board state
- Replace move-generation correctness
- Replace proper terminal-state detection
- Guarantee a win
- Change normal/hard difficulty except by improving search depth

18. Recommended Implementation Sequence

Step 1:
- Add TT data structures to module3.h.

Step 2:
- Implement Zobrist initialization.
- Implement state hash.
- Implement table clear, lookup, and store.

Step 3:
- Integrate TT lookup at negamax entry.
- Integrate TT store after completed search.
- Store TT best move.

Step 4:
- Integrate TT move ordering.

Step 5:
- Add TT generation reset to find_best_move().
- Prevent timeout search results from storage.

Step 6:
- Test TT-disabled vs TT-enabled on small boards.

Step 7:
- Add exact/lower/upper bound handling.

Step 8:
- Add incremental hash updates.

Step 9:
- Extend AIGameState and GameState for power-ups.
- Copy power-up flags through getBestMove().
- Include flags in Zobrist keys.

Step 10:
- Run randomized and power-up-specific tests.

19. Bottom-Line Assessment

Integration feasibility: HIGH

The existing architecture is compatible with a transposition table
because:

- The AI uses a copyable AIGameState
- Moves are already abstracted as Move
- MoveType already exists
- Negamax already receives a SearchContext
- Iterative deepening already exists
- The engine already separates frontend and AI state

The main risk is state completeness.

The TT must include every rule, board, player, and power-up state.
It must use correct exact/lower/upper bound handling and must never
store incomplete timed-out searches.

Once those rules are followed, a transposition table is one of the
most effective and low-risk improvements to the existing engine.
```
